d: $E(y-\hat f)^2=\text{bias}^2+\text{variance}+\sigma_\varepsilon^2$. Low SNR → variance dominates → prefer biased, stable models.
Orthonormal $X$: ridge $\hat\beta/(1+\lambda)$; lasso soft threshold $(|\hat\beta|-\lambda/2)^+$. Elastic net: sparse + grouping.
Labels, preprocessing, universe. Store knowledge time for every value.
train | purge (label horizon) | validate | embargo | train; final untouched test; preprocessing inside folds.
Proper CV → significance (DM) → strong baseline → stability → net Sharpe & correlation → complexity cost.
Average of $B$ correlated models: $\rho\sigma^2+(1-\rho)\sigma^2/B$. Bagging cuts variance; boosting cuts bias.
Maximum-variance directions; unsupervised (variance ≠ prediction); standardise; fit inside training data; loadings unstable when eigenvalues are close.
MDI, permutation, SHAP all split or hide credit. Use grouped permutation, ablation, conditional permutation, stability checks.
Ranking (AUC, rank IC) vs level (reliability, Brier). Sizing by magnitude needs calibration.
Prefer rank IC, net Sharpe, magnitude-weighted or portfolio-utility losses over accuracy.
Concept drift: $P(y\mid x)$ moves; covariate shift: $P(x)$ moves. PSI $=\sum(a-e)\ln(a/e)$, >0.25 large. Pre-set de-weighting and retraining rules.
Baseline ladder, point-in-time stamps, LLM training-cutoff check, residual IC over baselines, ablations, cost.

cards.q: $y=f(x)+\varepsilon$ and $\hat f$ is fit on a random training set. (1) Write the bias-variance decomposition of expected squared error at $x$. (2) What is special about financial prediction? (3) Which side of the trade-off do you lean to, and with what tools?
pts: (1) $$E\big[(y-\hat f(x))^2\big]=\big(E\hat f(x)-f(x)\big)^2+\mathrm{Var}(\hat f(x))+\sigma_\varepsilon^2$$ bias², variance, irreducible noise.
(2) Noise is over 99% of return variance ($R^2<1\%$), so flexible models fit noise and variance dominates; and the relation itself drifts (non-stationarity), so detailed fits break first.

(3) High bias, low variance: linear or regularised models, rank-transformed features, ensembles, strong shrinkage, early stopping, shallow trees, conservative validation (longer OOS, fewer hyperparameter searches).

cards.q: (1) Write the L1 and L2 penalties and their qualitative effect. (2) With an orthonormal design ($X^\top X=I$) and objective $\lVert y-X\beta\rVert^2+$ penalty, give both solutions in terms of $\hat\beta^{OLS}$. (3) Which do you prefer with many correlated predictors? (4) How do you decide in the end?
pts: (1) L1: $\lambda\sum|\beta_j|$, sparse (some coefficients exactly 0, feature selection). L2: $\lambda\sum\beta_j^2$, smooth shrinkage, all nonzero.
(2) Ridge: $\hat\beta^{OLS}/(1+\lambda)$ (proportional). Lasso: $\mathrm{sign}(\hat\beta^{OLS})\big(|\hat\beta^{OLS}|-\lambda/2\big)^+$ (soft threshold).

(3) Lasso tends to pick one member of a correlated group, and which one changes with the sample. Ridge spreads weight (identical columns get identical coefficients). Elastic net $\lambda_1\lVert\beta\rVert_1+\lambda_2\lVert\beta\rVert_2^2$ gives sparsity with a grouping effect.
(4) OOS performance and coefficient stability over time, not prior taste.

cards.q: (1) Define feature leakage. (2) Give three finance-specific examples. (3) At which levels of a pipeline can it occur? (4) What is the guiding principle?
pts: (1) Using information not available at the decision time, so the backtest beats what live trading can achieve.

(2) Revised or restated fundamentals, or aligning by fiscal period end instead of announcement date; today's index members or later delistings used to pick the past universe; full-sample z-scores, winsorisation, scalers or PCA. (Also: signal from the close traded at the same close; overlapping labels.)
(3) Label construction, preprocessing, universe construction. Model-level leakage is easy to spot; pipeline-level leakage is subtler.
(4) Point-in-time data: store for every value its knowledge time, not just the period it describes.

cards.q: Daily observations; the label at $t$ is the forward return $r_{t+1:t+20}$. (1) What is the problem with standard K-fold? (2) Describe the splitting scheme. (3) Explain purging and embargo. (4) What else must stay inside each fold?
pts: (1) It shuffles time, and neighbouring labels share 19 days, so validation and training share information.
(2) Time-ordered splits: walk-forward, or K-fold over contiguous time blocks; plus a final test period (e.g. the last 2–3 years) touched once.

(3) Purge: drop training samples whose label window $[t+1,t+20]$ overlaps the validation block (about 20 days before it). Embargo: leave a further gap after the block so feature autocorrelation cannot carry information back. Layout: train | purge | validate | embargo | train.
(4) Standardisation, feature selection and hyperparameter tuning are fit within each training fold only.

cards.q: A random forest beats a linear regression in cross-validation. (1) Do you deploy it? (2) List the checks you would run. (3) What could you do if the forest's edge comes from a few nonlinearities?
pts: (1) Not automatically: first confirm the win is real, stable and economically meaningful after costs.
(2a) Validity: was CV time-aware with purge/embargo (trees memorise local patterns, so leak more)? Is the gain significant (DM test on paired OOS losses, $t$ of the IC difference)?
(2b) Fair fight: was the linear baseline strong (rank / winsorised features, regularised)? Is the win stable by year, size, sector and regime?
(2c) Economics: net Sharpe after the extra turnover, correlation with existing signals, and the cost of complexity (interpretability, maintenance, drift sensitivity).
(3) Add those nonlinearities (e.g. a threshold term) to the linear model explicitly: more stable and interpretable.

cards.q: (1) Describe bagging and what it reduces; give the variance of an average of $B$ models with variance $\sigma^2$ and pairwise correlation $\rho$. (2) Describe boosting and what it reduces. (3) Why does gradient boosting work well on tabular financial data? (4) Risks and controls?
pts: (1) Train high-variance models (deep trees) in parallel on bootstrap samples and average: $$\mathrm{Var}=\rho\sigma^2+\frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2$$ Random forests also subsample features to lower $\rho$.
(2) Fit weak learners (shallow trees) sequentially, each to the negative gradient of the loss (residuals for MSE), added with learning rate $\eta$. Mainly reduces bias.
(3) Captures nonlinearities and interactions (cheap × high quality), invariant to monotone transforms (no scaling), handles missing values, fast.

(4) Overfits noise with many rounds or deep trees; fragile across regimes. Small $\eta$ + early stopping on a time-aware validation set, depth limits, row/column subsampling, larger minimum leaf size.

cards.q: $\Sigma=V\Lambda V^\top$ is a covariance matrix. (1) What is the $k$-th principal component? (2) Where is PCA useful in quant research? (3) What can go wrong? List at least four.
pts: (1) The eigenvector of the $k$-th largest eigenvalue: the direction of maximum variance orthogonal to the first $k-1$.

(2) Compressing correlated features (50 valuation ratios → 3 components); statistical risk models (top components ≈ market, sectors); denoising by dropping small-eigenvalue directions (random-matrix theory).

(3) Variance ≠ predictive power (unsupervised; signal can sit in low-variance components; consider PLS); unstable loadings when eigenvalues are close, and arbitrary signs; hard to interpret; leakage if fit on the full sample; scale-sensitive, so standardise first.

cards.q: Predictors are highly correlated. (1) Why are impurity (MDI), permutation and SHAP importances each misleading? (2) What more reliable approaches would you use?
pts: (1a) MDI favours continuous, many-valued features and splits credit randomly among correlated ones.
(1b) Permutation: the model recovers the same information from a correlated partner, so each looks unimportant; permuting also creates unrealistic feature combinations.
(1c) SHAP also splits credit among correlated features and depends on the background distribution.
(2) Cluster correlated features and permute or drop whole groups; ablation (retrain without a group, measure the OOS drop); conditional permutation; check rank stability across periods and seeds.

cards.q: (1) Define discrimination and calibration, with a metric for each. (2) Show they are separate properties. (3) When does a trading model need each?
pts: (1) Discrimination: are outcomes ranked correctly? (AUC = probability a random positive outscores a random negative; rank IC for continuous.) Calibration: do predicted levels match realised frequencies or sizes? (reliability plot, Brier score).
(2) Multiply every prediction by 0.5: the ranking is unchanged, calibration is broken.

(3) A cross-sectional long-short on deciles needs only ranking (rank IC). Sizing by magnitude (mean-variance $\mu$, Kelly, trade-or-not vs costs) needs calibration: a predicted 5 bp must really be 5 bp to compare with 3 bp of cost.

cards.q: (1) Why can maximising prediction accuracy be the wrong objective for trading? Give four reasons. (2) What objectives or metrics are better?
pts: (1) Ignores magnitude (55% right but the misses are the big drops); ignores ranking and portfolio construction (cross-sectional strategies need relative order); ignores costs (flipping predictions churn); class imbalance (predicting "flat" scores well).
(2) Rank IC, net-of-cost long-short Sharpe, magnitude-weighted losses, or a loss built from the downstream portfolio utility (decision-focused learning), with strong regularisation.

cards.q: (1) Define concept drift and distinguish covariate shift. (2) What would you monitor in a live model? (3) Give the PSI formula. (4) How should retraining or switching off be decided?
pts: (1) Concept drift: $P(y\mid x)$ changes over time. Covariate shift: $P(x)$ changes while $P(y\mid x)$ does not.

(2) Inputs (feature means, quantiles, missing rates); prediction quality (rolling IC / rank IC, hit rate, calibration error, residual mean); portfolio (P&L vs the backtest band, exposures, turnover, costs); all split by regime.
(3) $$\mathrm{PSI}=\sum_b(a_b-e_b)\ln\frac{a_b}{e_b}$$ $a_b$, $e_b$ = actual and expected bin shares; above about 0.25 is a large shift.

(4) By rules fixed in advance (e.g. rolling 12-month IC $t$ below a threshold → half weight; lower → switch off and review), and a fixed retraining schedule. Deciding in the middle of a drawdown is a fresh round of data snooping.

cards.q: An LLM scores financial text (filings, call transcripts) into a signal. (1) Which baselines would you compare against? (2) How do you handle timestamps? (3) What look-ahead risk is specific to LLMs, and how do you check it? (4) How do you measure incremental value? (5) Which ablations and costs matter?
pts: (1) Dictionary sentiment (Loughran-McDonald), TF-IDF + regularised linear model, pretrained embeddings + linear model, and known non-text signals (earnings surprise, analyst revisions, momentum).
(2) Use the actual release time (filing acceptance, call end); returns start at the next tradable time. Same universe, rebalance, neutralisation and cost model for every method.

(3) The training corpus may contain information from after the test date. Check: test only after the model's training cutoff, compare performance before vs after the cutoff, anonymise names and dates.
(4) Regress the LLM score on the baselines and earnings surprise; test the residual's rank IC and long-short returns, or its coefficient in a joint regression.
(5) Change the prompt or model, shuffle or truncate the text: sensitivity suggests a tuned result. Weigh API cost, latency and reproducibility (fixed model version, temperature).
